name: Mehran Sahami
title: Tencent Chair of the of the Computer Science Department, James and Ellenor Chesebrough Professor and Senior Fellow, by courtesy, at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies
research_topics: generative AI / LLMs in introductory programming courses
learning at scale and large-scale randomized education experiments
ethics, public policy and technological change
equity and global access in computing education
current_direction: Building generative AI into intro CS assignments rather than banning it (CS 106A 'Infinite Story')
Randomized-trial evidence on what LLM chat access does to engagement and exam outcomes at scale
Rethinking what CS fundamentals and assessment should look like in the AI era
Ethics, public policy and societal impact of technology (CS 182 / CS 182W, co-taught with Rob Reich)
Global-scale, human-centered CS teaching via the Code in Place model
current_direction_basis: Driven by four fetched 2025-2026 items: (1) the May 13, 2026 Stanford GSE / Stanford Report story in which Sahami is quoted as the CS 106A instructor defending AI use in the course ('rather than attempting to forbid use of AI until graduation, why not try to figure out what form of instruction creates a solid understanding of the material while taking advantage of these tools?') and on senior projects and equity of access; (2) the live CS 182 course site whose announcements page opens 'Welcome to the CS182 web site for Winter 2025-26!' with assignments running through March 17, 2026; (3) the 2025 ACM L@S paper 'The GPT Surprise', a 5,831-student / 146-country randomized control trial of GPT-4 access in an online coding class; (4) the 2025 SIGCSE paper 'Infinite Story', which is the same-named CS 106A assignment described in the 2026 news story. The Code in Place strand comes from the Stanford Engineering article naming Sahami as co-creator with Chris Piech. NOT based on his older biography (search/IR work at Google, CS2013 curriculum task force).

evidence.title: Stanford education experts put AI into perspective
evidence.summary: Stanford GSE / Stanford Report feature (May 13, 2026) built around Sahami's approach to generative AI in CS 106A. Quotes him directly: 'The tools do add productivity, industries are expecting students to use them, and students are going to use them, even if they are ‘banned’... So, rather than attempting to forbid use of AI until graduation, why not try to figure out what form of instruction creates a solid understanding of the material while taking advantage of these tools?' Also: 'By the time students get to their senior project, there's an expectation that they're using some AI tools to help produce that larger piece of work. That said, they have to have some fundamental knowledge to be able to assure that the code is doing the right thing.' Notes that CS 106A's AI lessons include ethics, bias and fairness, and that Sahami is an HAI faculty affiliate. Opens by describing the 'Infinite Story' assignment (code an adventure game from scratch, then use ChatGPT to keep it going).
evidence.venue: Stanford Graduate School of Education / Stanford Report (also mirrored at acceleratelearning.stanford.edu)

evidence.title: The GPT Surprise: Offering Large Language Model Chat in a Massive Coding Class Reduced Engagement But May Increase Adopters' Exam Performances
evidence.summary: Randomized control trial with 5,831 students from 146 countries in an online coding class, giving some students access to a GPT-4 chat interface. Per the OpenAlex abstract: estimates positive exam benefits for adopters, but 'the advertisement of GPT-4 led to a significant average decrease in exam participation,' with the effect modulated by country — 'Offering access to LLMs to students from low human development index countries increased their exam participation rate on average.' Authors: Nie, Chandak, Suzara, Malik, Woodrow, Peng, Sahami, Brunskill, Piech.

evidence.title: Infinite Story
evidence.summary: SIGCSE Technical Symposium 2025 paper (published 2025-02-18) by Piech, Sahami, Alonso, Liu, Arifov, Sreenivas, Webber, Zheng, Nguyen, Mlauzi, Woodrow — an 11-author paper with a large student author list. 'Infinite Story' is also the name of a current CS 106A assignment (visible on the CS 106A assignment list and described in the May 2026 Stanford GSE story) in which students code an adventure game from scratch and then use ChatGPT to extend it. No abstract was available from OpenAlex; the ACM DL landing page was not fetched.
evidence.venue: SIGCSE TS 2025 (ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education)

evidence.title: Code in Place — free global online CS106A-based course
evidence.summary: Stanford Engineering article: 'Chris Piech... co-created the project with colleague Mehran Sahami, professor and the Tencent Chair of the Computer Science Department.' Model is Stanford-led lectures plus ~10-student sections led by volunteer teachers; 'more than 30,000 learners have gone through Code in Place, which has had the support of about 3,000 section leaders.' The article is dated April 10, 2024 — this is the most recent Stanford-hosted page I could fetch about the program. The live site codeinplace.stanford.edu (fetched Aug 31, 2026) is a JavaScript app whose bundle enumerates course ids 'cip3','public','cip4','cip5','pylatino-25','cip6','cip7', indicating the program has continued past the 2024 article, but I could not fetch any rendered page text confirming the current cohort or its status.
evidence.venue: Stanford University School of Engineering news

undergrad_signals.signal: Large student co-author lists on his 2025 education papers
undergrad_signals.note: The 2025 SIGCSE 'Infinite Story' paper has 11 authors, most of them students (Alonso, Liu, Arifov, Sreenivas, Webber, Zheng, Nguyen, Mlauzi, Woodrow). I could NOT verify from any fetched page whether any of them were undergraduates at the time, so this is inference from author-list shape only, not a confirmed fact.

state_rationale: No fetched page contains a currently-open, undergraduate-relevant position for Sahami: he has no lab or group website (his old personal page at robotics.stanford.edu/~sahami/bio.html 404s, and the CS directory link cs.stanford.edu/people/mehran-sahami also 404s), the CURIS project API returned HTTP 401 so I could not check whether he has a 2026 project listed, and the only recruiting language I could actually fetch is department-wide advice on the CS undergraduate research page plus a 2024 Code in Place notice that says 'Applications for volunteer section leaders are closed.' At the same time the activity signal is strong and current: a May 13, 2026 Stanford GSE/Stanford Report feature built around his AI-in-CS106A approach, a live CS 182 site running through March 2026, and two 2025 peer-reviewed education papers. He is formally listed as instructor for CS 191/191W (senior project) and CS 199 (independent work), which is exactly the channel an undergraduate would use. That makes a cold email a reasonable, well-founded move — hence OUTREACH, not OPENING.
